This message comes from Angie. Angie has been helping homeowners find skilled pros
to get their home projects done well for over 30 years. For everything from minor repairs
to major remodels, find reviews, pricing, and booking at Angie.com or on the Angie app.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. In Alaska's Senate race, the Justice Department is
seeking to separate ballots cast for an unaffiliated candidate who has the same name as the incumbent
Republican Senator, Dan Sullivan. The DOJ says there's a risk the challenging Dan Sullivan's
candidacy will mislead voters. The New York Times reported that the Democratic candidate Mary
Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting the candidate. Peltola denies that. NPR has not
confirmed the report. A federal appeals court has rejected the Justice Department's request to set
aside thousands of California ballots, NPR's Jude Joffe Block reports. In a two-to-one vote,
a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel rejected the Trump administration's request. The Justice
Department wants California election officials to stop processing ballots pertaining to 20,000 people,
federal officials say, are likely non-citizens. But the accuracy of that list is in question.
The appeals court ruling upholds a federal court opinion from earlier this week. The majority
noted the Justice Department's last-minute request could disenfranchise eligible voters
and put the vote counting process in jeopardy. The same two judges had already ruled against
the Justice Department earlier in this case. A third judge dissented. Jude Joffe Block, NPR News.
Anti-Islam rhetoric in the Michigan Senate race has increased. NPR's Jason DeRose reports on the
Muslim community's response. Democrat Abdul Al-Sayed, who's Muslim, is facing Republican
candidate Mike Rogers. In recent days, President Trump has accused Al-Sayed without evidence of
being a jihadist and a member of the Islamist group the Muslim Brotherhood. Executive Director
of Michigan's Council on American Islamic Relations Dawoud Walid calls the accusations horrific.
In my 21 years of being with the Council on American Islamic Relations, I have never seen
this level of racism and anti-Muslim animus in our political discourse.
Walid says the Islamophobic rhetoric makes everyday Muslims feel dehumanized and afraid.
Jason DeRose, NPR News. A federal judge says he will be extremely frustrated if the DOJ arrests
former FBI Director James Comey while he's weighing arguments to dismiss the case,
and Piers Kerry Johnson reports. Lawyers for Jim Comey say prosecutors had 10 years to indict him
on allegations of leaking national security information in 2016. They say that time has
now come to an end and the judge should shut the door once and for all. Comey's lawyers say he
still faces possible arrest by the bureau he once led, which has had FBI agents stationed outside
his home. Judge Trevor McFadden told prosecutors not to conduct an early morning search, but the
judge seemed inclined to give prosecutors a bit more time to convince a grand jury to indict Comey.
Prosecutors say they're presenting new evidence, including an allegation from 2017, that could
extend the statute of limitations. Comey denies any wrongdoing. Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
Major U.S. stock indexes fell today. This is NPR.
Pope Leo says he voted in the U.S. midterm elections, casting a mail-in ballot in Chicago,
Meghan Williams reports. The Vatican says the Pope has exercised his right to vote as an American
citizen whenever he's been eligible. It also confirms he voted during his years living in Peru,
where he qualified to take part in elections there. The statement emphasizes the Pope's belief
that participating in democracy is both a right and a duty for citizens. Leo's vote is a reminder
that, along with his role as head of the Catholic Church, he retains his U.S. citizenship and
exercises his rights. For NPR News, I'm Meghan Williams in Rome. A small AI satellite launched
by Google earlier this month has answered its first query. NPR's Jeff Brumfield reports.
The AI chip circling above the Earth composed a haiku for humans back home. Blue marble below,
it wrote, "Data streams in silent grace. Starlight feeds my core." Followed by the
sparkles emoji because even in space, AI loves an emoji. The haiku was posted by Google CEO
Sundar Pichai on X. Google eventually hopes to build orbital data centers. The launch of this
chip is a small first step, but experts say a huge amount of work and potentially hundreds or even
thousands of satellites will be needed. Jeff Brumfield, NPR News. The Court of Arbitration
for Sport has ruled that Russian teams must be allowed to play international ice hockey
federation events such as the World Championships. The federation has barred Russian teams from its
World Championships since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. This is NPR News from Washington.
This message comes from Aura. A data breach may have exposed more than 153 million drivers licenses
in the U.S. A breach like that doesn't wreck your life by itself, but when someone uses your
information, the cleanup becomes your job. That's what Aura is for. Aura alerts you fast if your
info shows up in a breach, then locks your credit and provides U.S.-based fraud support 24/7.
